what_it_does: Modern processors execute instructions speculatively — they guess ahead rather than wait — but the Spectre family of attacks exploits this by tricking a processor into momentarily reading secret data and leaking it through subtle timing differences. Researchers have proposed defenses (called secure speculation schemes) that track which data touched during speculation is sensitive and restrict how it can be used, but these defenses had never been built into actual chip blueprints and tested at realistic hardware detail. ShadowBinding builds real chip-level implementations of two such defenses — STT (Speculative Taint Tracking, which marks sensitive data with a 'taint' flag and blocks tainted data from influencing observable behavior) and NDA (Non-Speculative Data Access, which simply delays memory reads until speculation is resolved) — on a real open-source processor design. A key finding is that the standard way of computing taint labels creates a bottleneck in the rename stage (the part of the chip that assigns register slots to instructions), so the authors move that computation later in the pipeline, recovering substantial speed at lower hardware cost.
